zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check after independent reading: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, licensed CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The returned transcription and review notes are separate scan-based work, not a reproduction of that index.

lines.note: Sabakite is the person who manages or negotiates, continuing the preceding page's sabaki entries. The scan supplies the missing t in the headword and the complete Portuguese Negociador and adminiſtra.
Sabi means rust. The first example describes wiping rust away, with the historical printed nogô retained; the Portuguese Alimpar is divided after A-.
Completes the rust-cleaning gloss and adds sabi wo migaku, polishing away the rust. The two examples share the same object, not separate senses of Sabi.
Otosu is offered as an alternative to migaku. Sabi ga tsuku then introduces becoming rusty, with the Portuguese Tomar beginning at the line end.

runs.text: mar ferrugem, ou fazer ſe ferrugento.

lines.note: Completes Tomar ferrugem and restates it as becoming rusty. The printed separation fazer ſe is retained in this Portuguese reflexive construction.
Sabi, sabiru, sabita gives the rusting verb's principal forms. The gloss explicitly applies it to iron, distinguishing the verb from the preceding noun.
Katana ga sabita means the sword has rusted. The Portuguese adjective ferrugenta continues below; catana is the historical Portuguese sword loan.

runs.text: genta. ¶ Itẽ, Estar algũa couſa ſolitaria ou

lines.note: Completes ferrugenta, then introduces a separate sense of being solitary. The source extends the verb beyond literal rusting.
Being unaccompanied completes the solitude sense. The following per met. introduces a figurative use; the scan shows deſacompanhada without the OCR's internal break.

runs.text: algũa couſa ja velha, ou çaſada, &c. ¶

lines.note: The figurative sense concerns something old or worn. The unusual printed çaſada is retained without supplying an expected nasal; Sa- begins the following Japanese example.

runs.text: Lugar, ou caſa que està ja velha,

lines.note: Sa- plus bita gives sabita tokoro, an aged or deteriorated place. The gloss specifies a place or house that has already become old.
The house is also described as damaged. This short conjunction phrase closes the figurative example rather than beginning the rusty-sword entry.
Sabigatana is a rusty sword, matching espada ferrugenta directly. The g reflects the printed compound and is not replaced by the separate noun katana.
Sabishii denotes a solitary condition or being alone. The source's paired noun-like and verbal Portuguese descriptions are preserved.
Sabishisa gives the corresponding noun and sabishuu an adverbial form. Both are upright Japanese forms; neither requires an invented Portuguese definition.

runs.text: Seta ferrugenta, ou ruim: palaura com

lines.note: Sabiya literally describes a rusty or poor arrow. The ensuing explanation concerns a soldier's self-deprecating use of the expression.

runs.text: q̃ algum ſoldado diz mal, ou deſfaz na ſua ſe-

lines.note: A soldier uses the phrase to disparage his own arrow modestly. The scan supports q̃ algum and deſfaz; the second consonant in deſfaz is f, not another long s.
Ta completes ſeta and the explanation closes with speaking humbly. It is self-deprecation by the soldier, not an accusation that another person's arrow is defective.

runs.text: Agoa dalgum pego, ou remanſo do

lines.note: Sabiye denotes water in a pool or quiet reach of a river. The scan supports remanſo; the final o of do is faint but its residual curve and the continuation rio support that reading.

runs.text: rio, que està turua por nam correr muito.

lines.note: The water is turbid because it does not flow much. The historical negative nam is retained rather than replaced by modern não.
Saburai denotes a nobleman or honorable man. The printed saburai is retained rather than replaced by the more familiar modern samurai.
The homonymous verb saburau is glossed as being or existing. Its principal forms retain their carons, and the upright S marks written usage.
Saka means a slope or incline. This complete short entry starts a new series and is independent of the preceding saburai forms.

runs.text: Ramo feito à maneira de vaſou-

lines.note: Sakabayashi is a branch arrangement made like a broom. Vaſou- is physically divided before the remainder of the Portuguese word below.

runs.text: ra, que ſe poem às portas das tauernas. No

lines.note: Completes vaſoura and locates the branch sign at tavern doors. No begins a regional usage statement on the next line.
The source says this is called Fote in Ximo. Both Ximo and Fote are Japanese terms within the Portuguese explanation; the capital X is visible.

runs.text: Compaßo ou modo de tanger deſcom

lines.note: Sakabyooshi describes playing out of time or in a contrary rhythm. The small caron over o is visible; deſcom continues below without an added hyphen.
Completes deſcompaßado and explains the performance as disordered and without consonance. The printed double-s ligature spelling is retained.

runs.text: Saco por onde ſe coa o arroz que

lines.note: Sakabukuro is the bag through which the rice mash is strained. The relative clause describing that rice continues on the next physical row.
The rice has already been made into the drink called vinho in the Portuguese gloss. The historical terminology is preserved instead of replaced by a modern brewing description.

runs.text: Copeiro, ou o que tem cuidado

lines.note: Sakabugyoo is the officer or attendant responsible for drink, compared to a cupbearer. The final long-vowel mark is a caron in this impression.
Completes the responsibility specified above: care of the wine or rice drink. The two-word continuation remains a separate physical row.

runs.text: Tina em que ſe eſpreme o arroz de

lines.note: Sakabune is the vat in which rice mash is pressed. The Japanese vessel name is explained through a Portuguese brewing comparison.
The rice is used to make the drink called vinho. This completes the definition of the pressing vat and introduces no separate operation.

runs.text: O voltear com os pès pera cima.

lines.note: Sakadachi describes turning upside down with the feet upward. The grave in pès is preserved rather than normalized to a modern accent.
Sakadachi wo suru illustrates performing this inverted movement or stance. The object particle remains attached in the printed Sacadachiuo.

runs.text: Mostras, ou reliquias deter bebido vi-

lines.note: Sakage denotes signs or traces of having drunk alcohol. The visible terminal mark after vi is a hyphen, continuing vinho on the next row.
Completes vinho, then quotes an emphatic denial of showing any sign of drinking. Mon. is an upright source label; the example's historical negative vorinai is retained.

runs.text: Por nenhum caſo tenho bebido vinho, nẽ ras

lines.note: The translation denies having drunk at all and begins denying even a trace. The printed nẽ is abbreviated, and no hyphen is added after ras.

runs.text: to, ou ſinal delleha em mĩ.

lines.note: To completes rasto; there is no trace or sign of the drink in the speaker. The tightly set delleha retains the scan's word spacing; the restored e and final mĩ correct the draft's missing vowel and mã.

runs.text: Cabelos da cabeça, que nacem aoreues.

lines.note: This entry concerns hair growing against its normal direction. The visibly printed final u in Sacagu and joined aoreues are retained rather than regularized from lexical expectation.

runs.text: Criança, que nace às aueſas. i, Com

lines.note: Sakago is a child born in reverse presentation. The explanatory i introduces the specification that follows, rather than another Japanese example.
The child is described as coming feet first. This completes the historical dictionary's definition without adding a modern medical classification.
Sakagura is a wine or sake storehouse. The letter after gu is r, correcting OCR Sacaguta; the Portuguese adega confirms the building sense.
Sakai means a boundary, border, or limit. The damaged initial is S, not B, and the following entry is a separate verb.
Sakai, sakau, sakauta describes opposing or contradicting. The printed abbreviated long-vowel forms retain carons and are not replaced by modern sakarau forms.
Itsumo hito no kotoba ni sakau hito ja describes someone who always contradicts others. The scan restores the missing t in fitono; the Portuguese translation begins in column 2.

runs.text: He homem que ſempre contradiz ao que os ou-

lines.note: This translates the previous column's example: a person always contradicts what others say. The scan reads contradiz, not OCR contraãiz; ou- continues below.
Completes outros dizem, then illustrates kokoro ni sakau. The new phrase concerns going against someone's feelings, with its Portuguese gloss continuing below.
The gloss completes the affront-to-the-heart expression. The next example offers kingen or chuugen, good or loyal counsel, and divides chǔ- at the physical edge.
Chuugen mimi ni sakau describes good counsel as disagreeable to the ear. The source begins its Portuguese paraphrase with good things or advice.

runs.text: bons conſelhos communmente não agradão aos

lines.note: The gloss states that good advice commonly does not please its hearers. Agradão is a single printed word, not the OCR's a gradão.
The ears complete the proverb's Portuguese wording. This single-word continuation belongs to the counsel example rather than the boundary noun below.
Sakaime is a border, boundary, or endpoint. The kind of land bounded is specified on the following physical row.
The definition applies to a plot, realm, or land. It completes Sacaime rather than introducing a dispute about such boundaries.
Sakairon is a dispute over demarcation. The Portuguese object of that demarcation continues onto the next row.
The disputed boundaries concern land or house plots. This closes the contention entry before the related term for reaching a settlement.
Sakai wadan denotes peace or an agreement about a boundary. The Portuguese fazem is divided after fa- at the right edge.

runs.text: zem os que confinão, ouſão vizinhos ſobre os

lines.note: The agreement is made by adjoining landholders or neighbors. The tightly joined ouſão is preserved as printed rather than silently respaced.
The settlement concerns the limits of plots or lands. This finishes the boundary-agreement definition.

runs.text: Contra marè, ou rolheiros da marẽ.

lines.note: Sakama is a contrary tidal current or eddy. The second tide word retains the draft's marẽ: its worn, compact mark is less distinct than the first marè, and is not normalized to match it.
Sakamaku is exemplified by waves or water running contrary to the current. Miz- continues as zu below; the printed double-z sequence is retained across the break.

runs.text: Ondas, ou agoas, que correm encon-

lines.note: Completes mizzu and begins the Portuguese explanation of opposing waves or waters. Encon- is divided before the next row's tradas.

runs.text: tradas, ou pera tras como rolheiros.

lines.note: Completes encontradas and compares the reverse-flowing water to eddies. The row finishes the sakamaku example rather than defining a separate current.
Sakamatsuge denotes eyelashes turned in the wrong direction. The description continues with how those hairs contact the eye.

runs.text: de maneira & encontrados, q̃entrão nos olhos.

lines.note: The lashes are turned so that they enter or press into the eyes. Maneira corrects OCR mancira; the abbreviated q̃ is not expanded in the transcription.

runs.text: O aueſo do pao, ou madeira que he

lines.note: Sakame concerns the reverse grain of wood. The relative clause explains the difficulty caused by working against its direction.

runs.text: difficultoſa de laurar por ir contra o direito das

lines.note: The wood is difficult to work because the cutting direction opposes its grain. The scan supports the doubled f in difficultoſa.
Veas completes the grain description. Sakame ni naru or iru introduces a figurative extension, with Per met. divided across the physical rows.

runs.text: met. Leuar a couſa não por razão, mas por co-

lines.note: The figurative sense is pursuing a matter not through reason but through anger. Co- begins colera on the following row.

runs.text: lera, ou teima, &c. como quãdo hum alterca,

lines.note: Completes colera and adds obstinacy, illustrated by someone arguing. The printed abbreviated quãdo is retained.

runs.text: & não ſe deixa leuar da razão, mas de ſua pai-

lines.note: The argumentative person follows personal passion rather than reason. Pai- is the first part of paixão on the next physical line.
Completes paixão and adds personal opinion. This closes the figurative against-the-grain sense before the defensive-obstacle entries.

runs.text: Huã maneira de eſtrepes de cana

lines.note: Sakamogari is a kind of pointed defensive obstacle made from cane. The tilde is visibly over the final a in Huã and is not moved to u.

runs.text: ou pao, ou ferro que ſe poem virados pera baixo

lines.note: Wood and iron are alternative materials, with the points directed downward. These details belong to the historical object description.

runs.text: ſobre o muro ao redor das fortalezas, ou de ou-

lines.note: The obstacles are placed above walls around fortifications or other enclosures. Ou- is divided before the next row's tras.
Completes outras cercas, extending the definition to other enclosed sites. The brief continuation does not belong to the following headword Sacamogui.
Sakamogi is explained by sakasama ni shigeru ki, trees or branches arranged upside down. The Japanese explanation remains upright and is not a Portuguese embedded-term toggle.

runs.text: ou aruores com os ramos, ou eſgalhos viradas

lines.note: The Portuguese identifies wood or trees with their branches turned downward. Its printed gender agreement is preserved rather than revised grammatically.

runs.text: pera baixo, q̃ poem amarradas a hũas eſtacas ao

lines.note: The branches point downward and are tied to stakes. The nasal marks in q̃ and hũas are retained; the sentence continues with the position of the defensive barrier.

runs.text: derredor das fortalezas, pera que os inimigos

lines.note: These stakes surround fortifications. The purpose clause introduces the enemy whose ascent the downward-pointing branches obstruct.
The obstacle prevents enemies from climbing freely. A paragraph mark introduces an example beginning Sacamogui; the printed double-s form in poßão is retained.

runs.text: Por eſtes paos, ou aruores com os

lines.note: Sacamogui uo fiqu means to set out this defensive timber. The Portuguese gloss begins with Por in its older infinitive use and continues the description of the branches.
The installation is explicitly described as having its branches downward. This completes the military sense rather than describing ordinary tree planting.

runs.text: Folguedo de muitos õde ha muito beber.

lines.note: Sacamori denotes a drinking gathering or party. The gloss stresses both numerous participants and abundant drinking; the nasal abbreviation õde is preserved.
The example turns the noun into an activity with ſuru. Beberetes refers here to drinking entertainments, not merely small individual drinks.
The alternative explanation again emphasizes a drinking party. The accent over hà is a grave mark, not the nasal mark transcribed in the draft.
Sacamucai is a welcoming refreshment sent to meet an arriving traveler. The scan reads the abbreviation &c., not &ca; the purpose of the refreshment continues below.

runs.text: manda ao encontro de quem vem por caminho

lines.note: The refreshment is sent out to meet someone approaching by land. The relative clause continues directly into the following line's alternative mode of arrival.
Arrival by boat is included alongside arrival by road. This short continuation finishes the definition of the welcoming refreshment.
Sacamuqe denotes hangnails or torn skin beside the nails. In this anatomical context eſpigas is figurative; the scan reads vnhas, correcting the draft's vnbas.
Sacan is illustrated by Sacan naru, to flourish or become prosperous. The Portuguese presents prosperity and vigor as related senses.
The gloss completes the sense of flourishing and being in full vigor. The terminal S. is kept outside the italic Portuguese as a separate printed label.

runs.text: Couſa de comer como carne, & peixe

lines.note: Sacana is introduced as something to eat, exemplified by meat and fish. The definition continues at the top of the next page; no closing punctuation is supplied here.
